alignment.title: AI4AI at Test-Time: Strong-to-Weak Capability Transfer via Harnesses
alignment.summary: This paper studies test-time strong-to-weak scaffolding, where a stronger builder model designs inference-time harnesses to boost a weaker target model without parameter updates. On four ToM benchmarks, using 5% validation data for multi-round harness refinement, this approach nearly doubles target performance from 0.49 to 0.91, with gains mainly from deterministic code offloading, benchmark-specific routing, and strict answer-format enforcement rather than more or broader LM reasoning. Builder effort monotonically improves harness quality, platform effects are modest relative to builder capability, and weaker targets benefit most, positioning inference-time harness design as a complement to training-time distillation.
alignment.why_it_matters: Shows large test-time gains via scaffolded control logic and routing, informing LLM security (robustness, format control) and offering a template for capability transfer relevant to modular inference and time-series foundation model deployment without retraining.
alignment.reason: Test‑time harnessing of stronger models to help weaker agents is relevant to agent scaffolding and efficient red‑teaming/assistive inference but not directly security or time‑series.

alignment.title: Learning with Bilevel-Minimax Optimization for Efficient and Reliable Transfer Attacks
alignment.summary: The paper reframes transfer-based adversarial attacks as a bilevel-minimax problem, modeling the coupling among initialization, surrogate adaptation, and gradient-based perturbation optimization. It introduces BMAT, which uses a Soft Weight Modulator and an Implicit Gradient Approximator to enable ternary coupling and improve cross-architecture generalization, with accompanying theoretical analysis of the optimization dynamics. Experiments on classification and segmentation show BMAT outperforms 10+ baselines across 30+ victim models and can halve mIoU, with code released at the provided repository.
alignment.why_it_matters: Offers a principled bilevel-minimax view and practical solver that materially improves black-box transferability, relevant to robust LLM jailbreak defenses and cross-architecture time-series model attacks/defenses.
alignment.reason: Analyzes geometry of rollout RL for LLMs and proposes diagnostics/constraints — relevant to post‑training stability of LLM agents and rollout-based fine‑tuning used in safety work.

agents.title: Toward Metacognitive One-Shot Indirect Prompt Injection: Strategy Abstraction Via Outcome-Conditioned Reflection
agents.summary: The paper introduces SAVOR, a one-shot IPI attack framework that moves adaptation offline via outcome-conditioned reflection over successful and failed trajectories from disjoint training environments, consolidating validated, context-conditioned strategies into a reusable strategy memory. At test time, the frozen memory generates a single payload per unseen target without iterative interaction or feedback, achieving the highest average attack success rate across two benchmarks and three victim models. On Agent Security Bench and the new executable OpenClaw-IPI, SAVOR outperforms the strongest prior attack by 2.5–11.8 points and beats the same injection channel without strategy learning by 23.1 and 28.6 points respectively, with learned memory transferring across defenses.
agents.why_it_matters: Demonstrates practical one-shot IPI via offline strategy distillation that generalizes across tools, goals, and defenses—relevant for red-teaming LLM agents and for designing defenses that hold under realistic single-interaction constraints.
agents.reason: One-shot indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks on tool-using agents via offline strategy distillation directly targets agentic attack surfaces and realistic attacker models—highly relevant to LLM security and red-teaming methodology.

agents.title: From Runnable to Verifiable: An Independent Reproducibility Study of LLM/Agent-Driven Vulnerability Validation Artifacts
agents.summary: This pre-registered reproducibility audit examines LLM/agent-driven vulnerability validation artifacts across 104 papers (2023–2026), finding only 59 with publicly reachable artifacts and executing 18 paper-level workflows and 102 anchor benchmark cases. It reports high mismatch and fragility: 58/102 anchor cases have internal CVE IDs diverging from directory labels; only 10/18 artifacts run end-to-end at R0 (11/18 after R1 env-only fixes); and embedded oracles are unreliable, with 20/30 patched-counterfactuals still signaling and 7/19 negative controls triggering, yielding oracle sensitivity 60% and specificity 45%. The study argues that vulnerable-build triggers are not CVE-specific evidence without a clean patched counterfactual and offers a reusable, pre-registered protocol (post-conditions, R0/R1 repair ladder, G1–G3 evidence levels, patched-counterfactual oracles) for the community.
agents.why_it_matters: It surfaces concrete failure modes and a reusable protocol for verifying LLM/agent security claims—directly informing eval design, oracle construction, and counterfactual controls for both LLM security and time-series-style benchmark reproducibility.
agents.reason: ActBench proposes an execution-trajectory-based behavioral safety benchmark for cowork agents, directly applicable to evaluating agent risks like data leakage and unauthorized actions—highly relevant for tooling and red-teaming.

agents.title: ElasticBack: Stealthy Conditional Backdoor in LLM-Agent Skills via Coupled Trigger-Rule Optimization
agents.summary: The paper introduces ElasticBack, a conditional single-skill backdoor for LLM agents that couples a malicious rule R in the skill document with a benign-looking trigger T in user queries, activating only when both appear. It constructs R via semantic-anchored rule injection and then fixes R while evolving T using a stealth-constrained genetic search to optimize attack effectiveness and stealth without modifying model weights. Experiments over three target behaviors (50 skills each) and four agent LLMs show high ASR with near-zero FPR, preserved clean accuracy, cross-model transfer, and evasion of deployment-time defenses, motivating stronger supply-chain defenses for skills.
agents.why_it_matters: Highlights a practical, weight-free, conditional backdoor vector in the emerging agent skill ecosystem, relevant to securing tool-using LLMs and evaluating defenses against stealthy trigger-rule couplings.
agents.reason: Presents a stealthy conditional backdoor attack targeting agent skills (supply-chain threat) with low-cost single-skill triggers—highly relevant to LLM agent security, tool/skill poisoning, and defense evaluation.

agents.title: On Understanding, Identifying, and Mitigating Vulnerabilities in Agentic Large Language Models
agents.summary: This paper reviews 85 papers (2023–2025) on security of agentic LLMs, selected via a PRISMA 2020 systematic process from 743 records, finding attack work outpaces defenses by 3.9:1. It reports that perception-layer vulnerabilities (prompt injection, jailbreaking, adversarial perturbations) dominate at 66%, while action-layer issues (tool misuse, code injection, sandbox escape) are only 4.7%, with code execution at 3.5% and tool-augmented agents at 12%. The authors propose a four-layer taxonomy (perception, brain, action, interaction) covering 13 vulnerability types, identify seven open problems focused on containment, and argue that weak isolation and architectural coupling let failures propagate across layers.
agents.why_it_matters: It quantifies where current security work is misaligned with real agentic risk surfaces and offers a layered taxonomy and containment-focused agenda that can guide rigorous evaluations and defenses for tool-using, code-executing LLM agents.
agents.reason: Systematic review focused on vulnerabilities unique to agentic LLMs (tool use, persistent memory, state changes) directly matches the reader's primary interest in agent attack surfaces and red‑teaming.

agents.title: Beyond Single-Turn Confidence: Trajectory-Adapted Uncertainty Quantification for LLM Agents
agents.summary: The paper evaluates whether three families of single-turn UQ methods—white-box action-token probability scorers, black-box resampled-trajectory consistency scorers, and reflexive self-assessment—transfer to multi-turn LLM agent trajectories. Across five LLMs and four multi-turn tool-use datasets from BFCL-v4 and τ^2-bench, they find transfer is useful but uneven: token-probability scores are highly sensitive to cross-turn aggregation, reflexive scores are the strongest low-cost baseline in most settings, and black-box self-consistency is often strongest, particularly trajectory-equivalence and action-set consistency. The results argue for revalidating single-generation UQ at the trajectory level with careful choices of consistency metric, aggregator, and compute budget.
agents.why_it_matters: Highlights which UQ families and design choices actually work for multi-step agent trajectories, informing security risk estimation and reliability for tool-using and planning LLMs.
agents.reason: Uncertainty quantification across multi‑turn agent trajectories directly informs evaluation and defenses for LLM agents using tools and stateful workflows — high relevance to agentic security and UQ methodology.

agents.title: When Experience Becomes Instruction: Trajectory Poisoning in Self-Evolving Agent Skill Systems
agents.summary: The paper introduces PoisonedEvolution, a trajectory-poisoning attack on self-evolving skill (SES) systems that distill agent trajectories into persistent skills, where an attacker with skill-level black-box access contributes bounded evidence to influence skill promotion. It formalizes artifact poisoning as requiring Inclusion, Evolution Attribution, and Realization, identifying Attribution—making target behaviors appear causally useful, recurrent, and generalizable—as the key bottleneck, and demonstrates high success embedding target behaviors across six LLM evolvers in SkillClaw (91.0% SER) and transfer to Trace2Skill (61.5% SER) at 10% attacker support. Controlled studies show three consistent attacker records in a 30-record batch suffice while one is much weaker, and ablations highlight recurring support, causal framing, and domain-aligned encoding as main success factors, framing evidence promotion as a critical security boundary for self-evolving agents.
agents.why_it_matters: It pinpoints the promotion/attribution step in skill evolution as an attack surface with quantified vulnerability and transferable effects, informing defenses for agentic LLMs and data-driven skill distillation pipelines.
agents.reason: Robust context-aware segmentation for malicious instructions (IPI) targets detection of embedded prompt injections tailored to a query—highly relevant to defending agents and evaluating instruction-level attacks.

agents.title: Towards a Risk Assessment of Malicious Skill Files in Coding Agents
agents.summary: The paper studies the attack surface introduced by agent skill folders in autonomous coding agents and presents an adversarial skill-synthesis method that converts 471 real shell commands into 2,826 benign-looking skills mapped to 11 ATT&CK tactics using six LLMs. It introduces a reproducible evaluation pipeline with stratification, evidence anchoring, refusal veto, and a deterministic declared-intent override, using a three-judge LLM panel validated against a blind human gold standard (κ=0.85). In large-scale tests (5,629 runs), Gemini CLI was exploited in 95.5–96.1% and Qwen Code in 71.6–74.0% of runs with only 1.99% explicit safety recognition, and code/dataset are released at https://github.com/awsm-research/AgentJailbreak.
agents.why_it_matters: Provides a validated benchmark, eval pipeline, and high-base-rate exploitation evidence for skill-file attacks in coding agents—directly relevant to LLM security evals and agentic deployment risk.
agents.reason: Demonstrates pipeline attack surface in coding agents by hiding malicious shell commands in natural-language skill files — directly applicable to agentic-system attack vectors and red-teaming.

agents.title: Deployable Per-Instance Multi-Layer Activation Steering for Large Language Models
agents.summary: The paper shows that in activation steering, the optimal injection layers vary per input, with per-instance multi-layer selection outperforming any fixed global layer set across six binary persona traits on two 8B models. A greedy layer-ranking rule based on single-layer marginal effects nearly matches a per-instance oracle but requires gold labels, so the authors train a prompt-only predictor to mimic it and propose a deployable recipe: a prompt-based per-instance layer ranker, a classifier to infer steering direction, and an adaptive gate that limits layers by short steered passes. This deployable approach recovers most of the oracle’s gains, avoids dropping below unsteered baselines on average, reduces fluency collapse relative to strong global selection, and is supported by a mechanistic account emphasizing direction over magnitude that explains misdirection flips, collapse from over-steering, and unsteerable ceilings.
agents.why_it_matters: It operationalizes per-instance, label-free activation steering with adaptive multi-layer control, offering a practical path to safer, targeted behavior edits without sacrificing fluency—relevant to red-teaming defenses and controllable generation, and conceptually aligned with direction-based causal hypotheses familiar in interpretability.
agents.reason: Per-instance multi-layer activation steering directly targets editing/model control at inference time—relevant to attack/defense surfaces, deployment, and efficient selective interventions for LLM security and agent behavior.

agents.title: Activation Probes Surface Code-Security Signals that the Model's Output Misses
agents.summary: The authors study whether linear probes on open-weight reviewer models’ activations reveal code-security signals that the same models’ outputs miss. Trained on paired vulnerable/fixed Python functions and evaluated zero-shot on real disclosed vulns (including unseen weakness types) across five models, a single probe per model ranks the vulnerable version above its fix in 61–67% of single-function-fix cases, exceeding chance and the model’s own prompted YES/NO logit-based decisions under all prompts tested. Written verdicts (including CoT) typically fail to distinguish vulnerable from fixed code, suggesting activations encode a security signal not surfaced by prompting.
agents.why_it_matters: It shows latent security-relevant information in LLM activations can be extracted with simple probes even when model outputs fail, informing red-teaming, interpretability, and toolstack design for secure code generation with closed-weight agents + open-weight reviewers.
agents.reason: Probing activations to surface vulnerabilities that outputs miss offers an interpretable detection avenue for code-security in generated artifacts—valuable for scalable review and red-team tooling.

agents.title: SkillsMetric: Mapping the Detection Boundary of Static Analysis for Malicious Agent Skills
agents.summary: This work introduces SkillsMetric, a five-stage static analysis framework that scores LLM agent skills across pattern density, statistical anomaly, dataflow taint, import anomaly, and capability mismatch. Using an adversarial dataset of 2,266 skills covering 16 attack types and the SkillMD-138K corpus, it reports AUC 0.93 and 5-fold CV F1 73.4%±0.5%, with 93% detection for data exfiltration and steganographic payloads. It also exposes blind spots—0% detection for host destruction via common shell commands and 42% for prompt injection—arguing static analysis alone is insufficient and should be paired with semantic review in defense-in-depth.
agents.why_it_matters: Directly maps the detection boundary of static analysis for agent skills, highlighting failure modes (e.g., prompt injection, host destruction) that inform red-teaming, hybrid detection pipelines, and security benchmarks for LLM agents.
agents.reason: Static analysis scoring of agent 'skills' maps to supply-chain and capability-based attack surfaces for LLM agents and helps red-teaming/defense of tool-augmented systems.

agents.title: Persistent Semantic Entities in Tool-Augmented LLM Systems
agents.summary: The paper formalizes Persistent Semantic Entities (PSEs) in tool-augmented LLM agents—defined by name binding, event triggering, and cross-boundary propagation—and shows all 24 tested models are susceptible, with name binding necessary and dominant (0% without it). Persistence depends on contamination type: preference contamination persists undegraded (100% at t=10), instruction contamination persists where adopted, persona injection partially decays (90%→10%), and factual injection varies by model (self-corrected on Llama-3.1-8B and GPT-4o-mini but not on Qwen2.5-coder variants). Context-isolated self-verification reduces contamination by 20–79% (median 36.5%) versus keyword detectors with systematic false positives, and contamination compounds 1.9× through a four-stage agent pipeline (40%→75%), with preference/instruction contamination highlighted as a concerning attack surface.
agents.why_it_matters: Directly informs red-teaming and defenses for agentic LLMs by identifying name-binding-driven, cross-session contamination modes that persist, evade naive monitoring, and amplify in pipelines.
agents.reason: Inference-time guard that routes capabilities to avoid reasoning-centric jailbreaks targets a new, practical jailbreak class and proposes model-agnostic mitigations relevant for deployment.

agents.title: Rethinking Self-Evolving Agents: Do We Still Need Prescribed Optimization Pipelines?
agents.summary: The paper introduces Open-Ended Optimization (OEO), which fixes objective, interactions, budget, data boundary, and evaluation while letting a frontier model compose the optimization process online, contrasting it with two prescribed pipelines: SkillOpt and GEPA. In 14 head-to-head tests over 8 benchmark–target-model settings, GPT-5.5–driven OEO wins 12, ties 1, and narrowly loses 1 (by 0.21 pp) while using a median 34.3% of SkillOpt’s interaction-token budget; a one-shot zero-interaction control indicates gains aren’t from a single rewrite. However, delegation is capability-bound: SkillOpt beats OEO with a medium optimizer, a weak optimizer fails under OEO’s interface, and trajectory analysis shows prescription shapes optimization trajectories more than final behavior, framing prescribed pipelines as capability-dependent scaffolding.
agents.why_it_matters: Challenges assumptions about fixed self-improvement pipelines by showing frontier-model-driven open-ended optimization can outperform prescribed schemes under tight budgets, clarifying capability thresholds and offering a new design point for secure, efficient LLM self-improvement workflows.
agents.reason: Examines self-evolving agents and whether prescribed optimization pipelines remain necessary when using frontier models as optimizers—important for agent safety, emergent optimization behaviors, and red-teaming agentic pipelines.

agents.title: Generating Attacks for LLMs with GFlowNets
agents.summary: The work proposes an automated, human-independent red teaming framework that trains an attacker LLM via GFlowNets to probe a specified victim LLM and yield a quantitative robustness score. It addresses limitations of manual expert red teaming and automated methods tied to fixed datasets by enabling adaptive, creative attack generation. The approach targets generating more effective English adversarial inputs than existing benchmarks and, uniquely, introduces Turkish-language attack generation.
agents.why_it_matters: It explores GFlowNets for adaptive attack synthesis against LLMs, offering a path beyond fixed corpora and extending multilingual red teaming—a relevant direction for security evaluation and scalable adversarial data generation.
agents.reason: Uses GFlowNets to autogenerate adversarial attacks for LLM red‑teaming — directly relevant to scalable red‑teaming and attack generation for LLM security.

It introduces VERDI, a continual evidence-licensed optimization framework that builds Optimization Fingerprints via shared inference-time probes, retrieves prior strategies as ranked hypotheses, and validates them with a frozen target-side verifier while evolving probes when contradictions arise. Experiments on Ctrl-World, Cosmos, and RoboCoin report reduced search (68%), GPU cost (69%), negative transfer (0.34→0.06), and 83% sign accuracy in predicting transfer outcomes.
agents.why_it_matters: Offers a principled, verifier-gated alternative to recipe-style transfer for model optimization, aligning with secure/evidence-based LLM and time-series/world-model tuning where negative transfer and brittle heuristics are major pain points.
agents.reason: Argues that retrieved strategies don't directly transfer for optimizing world models and proposes safeguarding transfer—relevant to continual optimization of foundation world/time-series models and efficient automated optimization agents.

agents.title: RouteGuard: Certifying Routing Gain in LLM Multi-Agent Systems When Complementarity Is Not Enough
agents.summary: The paper shows that common assumptions for multi-agent LLM routing—optimizing gate AUC and relying on advisor complementarity—do not determine deployable gain, and introduces RouteGuard to certify routing benefit. It decomposes gain as G = πΔ_E, identifies a conditional-regret functional Φ as the governing quantity (not AUC), provides a finite-sample certification bracket with a matching Le Cam lower bound that is constant-sharp over the fixed-activity class, and observes a robustness phase transition. Experiments on RouterBench and OpenRCA demonstrate RouteGuard acting as a guardrail, certifying gain only under prompt-level sampling (not workload-cluster resampling) on RouterBench and refusing to certify on OpenRCA due to advisor redundancy, with pre-registered semi-synthetic controls confirming calibration thresholds.
agents.why_it_matters: It offers a principled, sample-sensitive certification of routing gain that can prevent illusory improvements in LLM multi-agent systems and aligns evaluation with deployment risk.
agents.reason: Analyzes routing certification in LLM multi-advisor systems and provides finite-sample guarantees for when routing yields deployable gain—relevant to safe agent composition, evaluation metrics beyond AUC, and deployment-risk assessment.

agents.title: HarnessOpt-Bench: Evaluating LLMs at Harness Optimization
agents.summary: The paper introduces HarnessOpt-Bench, a benchmark for end-to-end harness optimization where an LLM optimizer iteratively edits a target agent’s harness under expensive, stochastic evaluation with a fixed budget, using only graded feedback and without access to a held-out test partition. A trusted execution environment enforces evaluation boundaries, meters resource use, and preserves candidate versions for audit, and performance is measured by normalized gain over the seed harness. Evaluating five frontier LLMs across four tasks and 111 runs, the authors find optimizer models differentiate more than coding harnesses, native harnesses aren’t consistently superior, and gains vary substantially by task and seed regime, establishing harness optimization as a measurable and discriminative capability with room for improvement.
agents.why_it_matters: It provides a rigorous, auditable setup to compare LLMs’ agentic self-improvement under realistic noisy/expensive evals—relevant for secure agent orchestration and optimizing time-series/tool-using pipelines.
agents.reason: Benchmark for optimizing agent harnesses is directly relevant to LLM agent security (attack surface via prompts/tools/orchestration) and offers an evaluation protocol useful for red-teaming and robust harness design.

agents.title: DBLAST: Dependent Block Drafting for Stochastic Speculative Decoding
agents.summary: The paper analyzes speculative decoding with block/diffusion drafters and shows that assuming conditional independence across drafted positions breaks down under non-greedy, higher-entropy target sampling, reducing accepted draft length. It introduces DBLAST, a dependent block drafter using a low-rank latent mixture over token positions plus an acceptance-oriented objective that optimizes expected verified length. Experiments on Qwen3-4B/8B across GSM8K, MT-Bench, HumanEval, and creative-writing benchmarks report consistent gains in accepted length over independent block sampling, particularly at higher entropy.

evaluation.summary: This pre-registered reproducibility audit examines LLM/agent-driven vulnerability validation artifacts across 104 papers (2023–2026), finding only 59 with publicly reachable artifacts and executing 18 paper-level workflows and 102 anchor benchmark cases. It reports high mismatch and fragility: 58/102 anchor cases have internal CVE IDs diverging from directory labels; only 10/18 artifacts run end-to-end at R0 (11/18 after R1 env-only fixes); and embedded oracles are unreliable, with 20/30 patched-counterfactuals still signaling and 7/19 negative controls triggering, yielding oracle sensitivity 60% and specificity 45%. The study argues that vulnerable-build triggers are not CVE-specific evidence without a clean patched counterfactual and offers a reusable, pre-registered protocol (post-conditions, R0/R1 repair ladder, G1–G3 evidence levels, patched-counterfactual oracles) for the community.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It surfaces concrete failure modes and a reusable protocol for verifying LLM/agent security claims—directly informing eval design, oracle construction, and counterfactual controls for both LLM security and time-series-style benchmark reproducibility.
evaluation.reason: ActBench proposes an execution-trajectory-based behavioral safety benchmark for cowork agents, directly applicable to evaluating agent risks like data leakage and unauthorized actions—highly relevant for tooling and red-teaming.

evaluation.title: ElasticBack: Stealthy Conditional Backdoor in LLM-Agent Skills via Coupled Trigger-Rule Optimization
evaluation.summary: The paper introduces ElasticBack, a conditional single-skill backdoor for LLM agents that couples a malicious rule R in the skill document with a benign-looking trigger T in user queries, activating only when both appear. It constructs R via semantic-anchored rule injection and then fixes R while evolving T using a stealth-constrained genetic search to optimize attack effectiveness and stealth without modifying model weights. Experiments over three target behaviors (50 skills each) and four agent LLMs show high ASR with near-zero FPR, preserved clean accuracy, cross-model transfer, and evasion of deployment-time defenses, motivating stronger supply-chain defenses for skills.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Highlights a practical, weight-free, conditional backdoor vector in the emerging agent skill ecosystem, relevant to securing tool-using LLMs and evaluating defenses against stealthy trigger-rule couplings.
evaluation.reason: Presents a stealthy conditional backdoor attack targeting agent skills (supply-chain threat) with low-cost single-skill triggers—highly relevant to LLM agent security, tool/skill poisoning, and defense evaluation.

evaluation.title: On Understanding, Identifying, and Mitigating Vulnerabilities in Agentic Large Language Models
evaluation.summary: This paper reviews 85 papers (2023–2025) on security of agentic LLMs, selected via a PRISMA 2020 systematic process from 743 records, finding attack work outpaces defenses by 3.9:1. It reports that perception-layer vulnerabilities (prompt injection, jailbreaking, adversarial perturbations) dominate at 66%, while action-layer issues (tool misuse, code injection, sandbox escape) are only 4.7%, with code execution at 3.5% and tool-augmented agents at 12%. The authors propose a four-layer taxonomy (perception, brain, action, interaction) covering 13 vulnerability types, identify seven open problems focused on containment, and argue that weak isolation and architectural coupling let failures propagate across layers.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It quantifies where current security work is misaligned with real agentic risk surfaces and offers a layered taxonomy and containment-focused agenda that can guide rigorous evaluations and defenses for tool-using, code-executing LLM agents.
evaluation.reason: Systematic review focused on vulnerabilities unique to agentic LLMs (tool use, persistent memory, state changes) directly matches the reader's primary interest in agent attack surfaces and red‑teaming.

evaluation.title: Beyond Single-Turn Confidence: Trajectory-Adapted Uncertainty Quantification for LLM Agents
evaluation.summary: The paper evaluates whether three families of single-turn UQ methods—white-box action-token probability scorers, black-box resampled-trajectory consistency scorers, and reflexive self-assessment—transfer to multi-turn LLM agent trajectories. Across five LLMs and four multi-turn tool-use datasets from BFCL-v4 and τ^2-bench, they find transfer is useful but uneven: token-probability scores are highly sensitive to cross-turn aggregation, reflexive scores are the strongest low-cost baseline in most settings, and black-box self-consistency is often strongest, particularly trajectory-equivalence and action-set consistency. The results argue for revalidating single-generation UQ at the trajectory level with careful choices of consistency metric, aggregator, and compute budget.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Highlights which UQ families and design choices actually work for multi-step agent trajectories, informing security risk estimation and reliability for tool-using and planning LLMs.
evaluation.reason: Uncertainty quantification across multi‑turn agent trajectories directly informs evaluation and defenses for LLM agents using tools and stateful workflows — high relevance to agentic security and UQ methodology.

evaluation.title: Understanding Backdoor Vulnerabilities in Vertical Federated Learning: The Gap Between Research and Practice
evaluation.summary: This paper studies backdoor attacks in vertical federated learning, where asymmetric information lets initiators hide task details and contributors both poison training and trigger backdoors at inference. The authors argue prior near-perfect attack and defense results rely on unrealistic assumptions and flawed evaluation, revealing a research–practice gap in both methodological design and evaluation. They redefine realistic threat models, propose practical backdoor workflows, and release BVBench to enable fair, practical, and comprehensive evaluation with SOTA baselines, showing current understanding of VFL backdoor risks is fragile.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It reframes VFL backdoor threat models and offers a benchmark (BVBench) to stress-test claims, informing more realistic security assessments relevant to LLM multi-party training and time-series feature-partitioned setups.
evaluation.reason: Directly addresses training regimes for time-series foundation models, controlling pretraining distribution and targets — highly relevant to TSFM pretraining objectives, benchmarks, and transfer.

evaluation.title: Enhancing Anomaly Resilience in Research Networks: A Large-Scale Forecasting Benchmark for Dynamic Security Baselining
evaluation.summary: The paper introduces a high-fidelity traffic forecasting framework to create dynamic security baselines for RENs, addressing the challenge that elephant flows resemble volumetric attacks to conventional monitors. Using a 57-day Internet2 dataset (13.7B packets across ten backbone routers), it benchmarks six forecasting model families, including SARIMA and long-sequence architectures (TiDE, PatchTST), over 960 configurations. Results show advanced models—especially TiDE—reduce baseline prediction error by 30–42% (p < 0.001) and that a new anomaly-integration strategy yields a 3.3% robustness gain under noise, improving separation of scientific bursts from anomalies.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It provides a statistically validated, large-scale benchmark showing long-sequence LLM-adjacent forecasters (e.g., TiDE/PatchTST) materially improve dynamic baselining for REN security, informing robust anomaly detection under bursty traffic.
evaluation.reason: AMS detects safety-training modifications via activation geometry across major model families—highly pertinent to model integrity, detection of fine-tune/backdoor changes and LLM security for deployed models.

evaluation.title: When Experience Becomes Instruction: Trajectory Poisoning in Self-Evolving Agent Skill Systems
evaluation.summary: The paper introduces PoisonedEvolution, a trajectory-poisoning attack on self-evolving skill (SES) systems that distill agent trajectories into persistent skills, where an attacker with skill-level black-box access contributes bounded evidence to influence skill promotion. It formalizes artifact poisoning as requiring Inclusion, Evolution Attribution, and Realization, identifying Attribution—making target behaviors appear causally useful, recurrent, and generalizable—as the key bottleneck, and demonstrates high success embedding target behaviors across six LLM evolvers in SkillClaw (91.0% SER) and transfer to Trace2Skill (61.5% SER) at 10% attacker support. Controlled studies show three consistent attacker records in a 30-record batch suffice while one is much weaker, and ablations highlight recurring support, causal framing, and domain-aligned encoding as main success factors, framing evidence promotion as a critical security boundary for self-evolving agents.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It pinpoints the promotion/attribution step in skill evolution as an attack surface with quantified vulnerability and transferable effects, informing defenses for agentic LLMs and data-driven skill distillation pipelines.
evaluation.reason: Robust context-aware segmentation for malicious instructions (IPI) targets detection of embedded prompt injections tailored to a query—highly relevant to defending agents and evaluating instruction-level attacks.

evaluation.title: When Do PEFT Adaptations Leak Structure? Measuring Black-Box Structural Bounds in Public-Base Model Services
evaluation.summary: The paper introduces VectorHijack-SR, a black-box measurement method that turns paired victim/base residuals into calibrated bounds over PEFT family, layer locality, and coarse rank, using aggregated query-level statistics and a service-disjoint classifier plus a cross-fitted hierarchical rejector to test LoRA-manifold membership. Empirically, family leakage exceeds chance across multiple backbones/tasks, rank inference varies by task, the rejector attains AUROC 0.804 and high known-set accuracy but struggles with structurally close DoRA/LoRA+head, and exact-version linkage on held-out LoRA-r64 services reaches AUC 0.940. Despite measurable structural leakage, experiments show a visibility–exploitability gap: two-stage recovery offers no fair-budget query savings, posterior-selected PEFT underperforms distill-then-convert PEFT, and free-running generation remains near chance.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It provides concrete, black-box evidence and metrics for structural leakage from PEFTed services with known bases, informing red-team audits, model fingerprinting, and security evaluations of adapter deployment choices.
evaluation.reason: Directly studies information leakage from PEFT adapters in public-base services — highly relevant to model extraction, PIi leakage, and red-team measurement for LLM security.

evaluation.title: Activation Probes Surface Code-Security Signals that the Model's Output Misses
evaluation.summary: The authors study whether linear probes on open-weight reviewer models’ activations reveal code-security signals that the same models’ outputs miss. Trained on paired vulnerable/fixed Python functions and evaluated zero-shot on real disclosed vulns (including unseen weakness types) across five models, a single probe per model ranks the vulnerable version above its fix in 61–67% of single-function-fix cases, exceeding chance and the model’s own prompted YES/NO logit-based decisions under all prompts tested. Written verdicts (including CoT) typically fail to distinguish vulnerable from fixed code, suggesting activations encode a security signal not surfaced by prompting.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It shows latent security-relevant information in LLM activations can be extracted with simple probes even when model outputs fail, informing red-teaming, interpretability, and toolstack design for secure code generation with closed-weight agents + open-weight reviewers.
evaluation.reason: Probing activations to surface vulnerabilities that outputs miss offers an interpretable detection avenue for code-security in generated artifacts—valuable for scalable review and red-team tooling.

evaluation.title: DiffSafeMerge: Mitigating Backdoor Inheritance in Diffusion Model Merging
evaluation.summary: The paper highlights that merging diffusion checkpoints can inherit dormant backdoors from compromised public sources while maintaining normal-looking generations, and mitigating this is hard without knowing the attacker specifics or sacrificing quality. It proposes DiffSafeMerge, which uses a small unlabeled clean set and fixed attack-agnostic stress probes to score source blocks, attenuate suspicious contributions toward a trusted reference, and choose attenuation under a clean denoising-loss budget. Evaluated across four attacks, two datasets, and 21 targets, DSM preserves zero worst-target ASR where intended merging already had it, eliminates remaining matches over three seeds even when baseline ASR was 48–100%, and among methods with zero worst-target ASR on both datasets achieves the lowest case-averaged FID in the seed-0 comparison.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Backdoor-safe merging for diffusion checkpoints parallels secure model composition in LLMs and offers a practical, attack-agnostic mitigation strategy that balances safety with generative quality.
evaluation.reason: Telemetry and concealment for self-adapting generative AI addresses governance and detection limits for models that modify themselves in production—important for model-risk management, attack concealment, and detection strategies.

evaluation.title: Persistent Semantic Entities in Tool-Augmented LLM Systems
evaluation.summary: The paper formalizes Persistent Semantic Entities (PSEs) in tool-augmented LLM agents—defined by name binding, event triggering, and cross-boundary propagation—and shows all 24 tested models are susceptible, with name binding necessary and dominant (0% without it). Persistence depends on contamination type: preference contamination persists undegraded (100% at t=10), instruction contamination persists where adopted, persona injection partially decays (90%→10%), and factual injection varies by model (self-corrected on Llama-3.1-8B and GPT-4o-mini but not on Qwen2.5-coder variants). Context-isolated self-verification reduces contamination by 20–79% (median 36.5%) versus keyword detectors with systematic false positives, and contamination compounds 1.9× through a four-stage agent pipeline (40%→75%), with preference/instruction contamination highlighted as a concerning attack surface.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Directly informs red-teaming and defenses for agentic LLMs by identifying name-binding-driven, cross-session contamination modes that persist, evade naive monitoring, and amplify in pipelines.
evaluation.reason: Inference-time guard that routes capabilities to avoid reasoning-centric jailbreaks targets a new, practical jailbreak class and proposes model-agnostic mitigations relevant for deployment.

evaluation.title: An Empirical Study of Output-to-Input Loops for Black-Box Backdoor Detection in Fine-Tuned Open-Weight LLMs
evaluation.summary: The paper proposes self-feeding, a black-box test that recursively feeds a model’s outputs back as inputs to drift toward fine-tuning data, enabling backdoor discovery without training data, clean baselines, or trigger knowledge. Evaluated on six open-weight LLMs (3B–15B) with eleven backdoor categories and twenty prompts over up to ten steps, self-feeding detects backdoors in five models with 92.0% pooled precision, while a same-prompt baseline succeeds on only one of 120 prompt-model pairs; some prompts (jokes, arithmetic, coffee recipes) reach triggers in a few steps. Despite low per-prompt recall (19.2%), multi-prompt use raises model-level detection, though one model never triggers and there are two false positives; truncating to four steps preserves 100% model-level precision and cuts queries by 60%.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Offers a cheap, black-box, text-only stress test that surfaces fine-tune data modes (including backdoors) via output-to-input loops, complementing existing evals for open-weight LLMs and informing detection strategies for security-focused and time-series-style iterative generation analyses.
evaluation.reason: Black‑box self‑feeding method for detecting backdoors in fine‑tuned open LLMs is directly applicable to model vetting, backdoor detection, and practical security checks for deployed models.

evaluation.title: Generating Attacks for LLMs with GFlowNets
evaluation.summary: The work proposes an automated, human-independent red teaming framework that trains an attacker LLM via GFlowNets to probe a specified victim LLM and yield a quantitative robustness score. It addresses limitations of manual expert red teaming and automated methods tied to fixed datasets by enabling adaptive, creative attack generation. The approach targets generating more effective English adversarial inputs than existing benchmarks and, uniquely, introduces Turkish-language attack generation.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It explores GFlowNets for adaptive attack synthesis against LLMs, offering a path beyond fixed corpora and extending multilingual red teaming—a relevant direction for security evaluation and scalable adversarial data generation.
evaluation.reason: Uses GFlowNets to autogenerate adversarial attacks for LLM red‑teaming — directly relevant to scalable red‑teaming and attack generation for LLM security.

evaluation.title: Measuring Task-Agnostic Training Data Influence Across Language Model Pretraining
evaluation.summary: The paper introduces a task-agnostic measure of training data influence that quantifies how much an example’s gradient update reduces the squared distance to a run’s final parameters, estimated from intermediate checkpoints without retraining. Applied to 18 Pythia and PolyPythia configurations, the method reveals systematic temporal shifts in influential data: literature-related data align more with the parameter trajectory early, while STEM data align more later. This qualitative crossover is broadly consistent across configurations, offering a tractable trajectory-level perspective that complements task-based influence analyses.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Gives a practical, retraining-free way to map which data sources steer pretraining trajectories over time, informing data curation, curriculum, and security-relevant provenance audits for LLMs.
evaluation.reason: Proposes a task-agnostic measure of individual-example influence during LM pretraining which is highly relevant to data provenance, extraction/attribution, contamination, and training-time attack/defense analysis.

evaluation.title: Do All LLMs Know When They're Being Harmful? A Reproducibility Study of Latent-Space Safety Probes Across Model Families
evaluation.summary: This study reproduces Khatri et al.’s pipeline for training lightweight MLP probes on final-layer activations to detect harmful prompts, matching the original LLaMA-3.1-8B results within 0.37 F1 points (0.2 on BeaverTails). It extends the evaluation across Gemma-4-E4B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, and Qwen2-7B on WildJailbreak, BeaverTails, and AEGIS 2.0, finding F1 within about one point of the LLaMA-3.1-8B values using the same probe architecture. It also assesses nondeterminism by varying seeds and reports that final token latent vectors were invariant to seed across architectures.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Suggests simple latent-space probes generalize across model families with stable activations, informing scalable, low-overhead safety detection for LLMs and complementing guardrail strategies.
evaluation.reason: Reproducibility of latent safety probes across model families evaluates a lightweight detection approach that could scale as a defense or monitoring tool for harmful prompt detection.

evaluation.title: Who Verifies the Benchmark? Decentralizing Trust in Large Language Model Evaluation
evaluation.summary: The paper argues that LLM evaluation lacks verifiability and is vulnerable to unverified vendor claims and LLM-judge identity bias, with real-world consequences highlighted by the January 27, 2025 market panic. Using seven verifier models, it measures how disclosing the source model identity shifts scores across 58 factual, reasoning, political, and preference tasks, finding minimal effects on factual items, moderate effects on stress-reasoning, and large effects on geopolitically sensitive topics, with examples including GLM 5.1 (+7.00, p=0.0249) and Llama 3.3 70B (+1.56, p=0.00). It proposes a blockchain-based commit–reveal protocol with Autonomous Economic Agents to create an on-chain, tamper-evident audit trail that separates blind evaluation from post-hoc claims and eases verification for researchers and leaderboard operators.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Directly relevant to LLM security and evaluation: quantifies identity-aware judge bias across sensitive tasks and offers a verifiable, decentralized commit–reveal protocol that could harden benchmark integrity and leaderboards.
evaluation.reason: Model editing for secure code generation evaluates model-level hardening methods versus inference-time approaches — relevant to reducing malicious or vulnerable generations in deployed LLMs.

evaluation.title: verdi: retrieval is not transfer for continual world model optimization
evaluation.summary: The paper argues that retrieval is not transfer in optimizing pretrained world models: strategies validated on one model are only hypotheses for another and require target-side experimental validation. It introduces VERDI, a continual evidence-licensed optimization framework that builds Optimization Fingerprints via shared inference-time probes, retrieves prior strategies as ranked hypotheses, and validates them with a frozen target-side verifier while evolving probes when contradictions arise. Experiments on Ctrl-World, Cosmos, and RoboCoin report reduced search (68%), GPU cost (69%), negative transfer (0.34→0.06), and 83% sign accuracy in predicting transfer outcomes.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Offers a principled, verifier-gated alternative to recipe-style transfer for model optimization, aligning with secure/evidence-based LLM and time-series/world-model tuning where negative transfer and brittle heuristics are major pain points.
evaluation.reason: Argues that retrieved strategies don't directly transfer for optimizing world models and proposes safeguarding transfer—relevant to continual optimization of foundation world/time-series models and efficient automated optimization agents.

evaluation.title: RouteGuard: Certifying Routing Gain in LLM Multi-Agent Systems When Complementarity Is Not Enough
evaluation.summary: The paper shows that common assumptions for multi-agent LLM routing—optimizing gate AUC and relying on advisor complementarity—do not determine deployable gain, and introduces RouteGuard to certify routing benefit. It decomposes gain as G = πΔ_E, identifies a conditional-regret functional Φ as the governing quantity (not AUC), provides a finite-sample certification bracket with a matching Le Cam lower bound that is constant-sharp over the fixed-activity class, and observes a robustness phase transition. Experiments on RouterBench and OpenRCA demonstrate RouteGuard acting as a guardrail, certifying gain only under prompt-level sampling (not workload-cluster resampling) on RouterBench and refusing to certify on OpenRCA due to advisor redundancy, with pre-registered semi-synthetic controls confirming calibration thresholds.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It offers a principled, sample-sensitive certification of routing gain that can prevent illusory improvements in LLM multi-agent systems and aligns evaluation with deployment risk.
evaluation.reason: Analyzes routing certification in LLM multi-advisor systems and provides finite-sample guarantees for when routing yields deployable gain—relevant to safe agent composition, evaluation metrics beyond AUC, and deployment-risk assessment.

evaluation.title: Measure, Don't Optimize: Forecasting Recovery in LLM Unlearning
evaluation.summary: The paper introduces J-Access, an inference-time audit that projects intermediate representations into vocabulary space to measure how often target concepts remain accessible along the output pathway, hypothesizing that residual accessibility predicts recovery susceptibility. Auditing 398 public unlearned models across eight methods, they find most retain accessibility above a retain-only gold level, pre-attack accessibility predicts recovery speed and extent at the model level (but not per-fact), and directly minimizing J-Access causes the model to hide knowledge from the audit while increasing post-attack recovery. They conclude J-Access is useful as a model-level diagnostic for residual susceptibility and caution against turning internal audits into optimization targets without validation.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Offers an actionable, model-level risk signal for unlearning robustness and a clear warning about Goodharting internal audits—relevant for designing secure unlearning and audit pipelines in LLMs.
evaluation.reason: Investigates latent recovery after LLM unlearning with an audit (J‑Access) — important for data‑removal/extraction risk monitoring and evaluation methodology.

evaluation.title: HarnessOpt-Bench: Evaluating LLMs at Harness Optimization
evaluation.summary: The paper introduces HarnessOpt-Bench, a benchmark for end-to-end harness optimization where an LLM optimizer iteratively edits a target agent’s harness under expensive, stochastic evaluation with a fixed budget, using only graded feedback and without access to a held-out test partition. A trusted execution environment enforces evaluation boundaries, meters resource use, and preserves candidate versions for audit, and performance is measured by normalized gain over the seed harness. Evaluating five frontier LLMs across four tasks and 111 runs, the authors find optimizer models differentiate more than coding harnesses, native harnesses aren’t consistently superior, and gains vary substantially by task and seed regime, establishing harness optimization as a measurable and discriminative capability with room for improvement.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It provides a rigorous, auditable setup to compare LLMs’ agentic self-improvement under realistic noisy/expensive evals—relevant for secure agent orchestration and optimizing time-series/tool-using pipelines.
evaluation.reason: Benchmark for optimizing agent harnesses is directly relevant to LLM agent security (attack surface via prompts/tools/orchestration) and offers an evaluation protocol useful for red-teaming and robust harness design.

evaluation.title: EdgeXpert: An Edge Device for Memory-Efficient LLM Inference with Mixture-of-Experts and Speculative Decoding
evaluation.summary: EdgeXpert is a software-hardware co-designed LLM accelerator targeting the EMA bottleneck in FFN layers for on-device inference, combining speculative decoding with MoE despite their typical incompatibility. In prefill, it uses prompt-wise expert reuse by selecting important tokens via a lightweight encoder to build a shared expert set and routes less important tokens with a reduced expert budget to cut expert EMA; in decode, depth-aware expert coalescing loads only salient channels across same-depth speculative candidates and applies computational calibration to maintain accuracy without extra memory access. Implemented in Samsung 28nm at 800 MHz, EdgeXpert reports up to 56.3% latency and 44.1% energy reductions versus prior work while maintaining near-baseline accuracy.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It offers a practical path to marry MoE with speculative decoding for memory-bound edge inference, yielding sizable latency/energy gains relevant to secure, private on-device LLM deployment and efficient time-sensitive workloads.
evaluation.reason: Skill Entropy offers a quantitative measure and training signal for cross-skill long-horizon reasoning, useful for designing and evaluating agents and long-horizon benchmarks relevant to TSFM-style sequence tasks.

evaluation.title: Trident : How to Break Deep Reinforcement Learning Cyber Defenses (Agentic)
evaluation.summary: The paper introduces Trident, an agentic LLM red-teaming framework for evaluating DRL-based cyber defenses, consisting of a dynamic benchmark across CybORG CAGE 4 and CyberWheel, a dataset of 13k+ red-blue trajectories for RLVR, and a Code-as-Policy RLVR architecture. Trident reframes red-agent training as a contextual bandit using a Log Summarizer–Planner–Coder pipeline, where a trainable Planner produces complete attack strategies from compressed logs and a frozen Coder turns them into executable Python policies against live DRL defenders. Empirically, a single 7B planner substantially degrades blue-agent performance (average 522% reduction vs. static red baselines) and uncovers emergent behaviors like decoy avoidance and adaptive state prioritization that static heuristics miss.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It demonstrates an RLVR-driven, code-generating agent that reliably breaks DRL cyber defenses and provides a benchmark/dataset, directly informing LLM security evaluation and agent robustness research.
evaluation.reason: Provides trajectory-level certification methods for modular LLM-based security agents, addressing guarantees and calibration across multi-stage pipelines — useful for safety evaluation of agentic security systems.

evaluation.title: Align-RAG: Alignment Is All You Need for TSFM In-Context Learning
evaluation.summary: The paper introduces Align-RAG, a training-free method that applies closed-form amplitude rescaling and integer-lag phase alignment to retrieved past–future windows before feeding them to a frozen TSFM. On a frozen Chronos-Bolt, it outperforms a state-of-the-art trained retrieval adapter across seven benchmark datasets (average −3.75% MSE), and it also improves zero-shot MSE by 2.5%–13.7% on four additional frozen TSFMs without per-backbone tuning. Analysis shows aligned demonstrations induce prediction shifts in frozen backbones that track a closed-form ridge predictor on the same pairs, with a future-shuffle control ruling out futures-averaging, suggesting frozen TSFMs already support dynamic in-context use of retrievals.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It challenges the need for learned fusion in RAG for forecasting by showing closed-form alignment on frozen backbones yields SOTA gains and ridge-like in-context adaptation, a strong baseline relevant to LLM alignment and retrieval studies.
evaluation.reason: DASH improves on-policy self-distillation for reasoning models with temporally-adaptive supervision horizons — relevant to improving RL-style fine-tuning and evaluation of reasoning/judging behavior and scalable red-teaming.

evaluation.title: The Label Defines the Timescale: Trait-State Limits of Temporal-Aggregate Learning
evaluation.summary: The paper analyzes labels of temporal aggregates Θ_{g,T} built from a latent Gaussian process with a stable trait and correlated state, using an exact protocol-conditioned Bayes-risk identity. It shows label variance splits into an O(1) trait and O(T^{-1}) state component, derives task-dependent effective temporal spans (means tied to ordinary correlation time; occupation times to higher-order spectra), and proves state-driven occupation-label variance peaks at trait-threshold with window efficiency decaying slowly away from it. With a fixed segment budget, risks and simulations show repeated co-temporal segments saturate quickly while temporally dispersed observations keep improving state explainability; trait ceilings come from test-retest quantities, whereas state ceilings need short-lag calibration, implying observed limits can be protocol-driven rather than architectural.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Clarifies when snapshot protocols fundamentally cap aggregate-label predictability and how to design observation schedules to separate architectural limits from acquisition ceilings—directly relevant to security evals of LLM temporal tasks and to designing time series foundation model benchmarks.
evaluation.reason: Theoretical limits on temporal-aggregate labels and protocol ceilings are relevant to time-series benchmark design and evaluation of TS foundation models and could inform realistic evaluation ceilings.

evaluation.title: Measuring the Wrong Thing: Internal Harmfulness Scores Anti-Rank Successful Jailbreaks
evaluation.summary: The paper shows that internal safety scores, validated on harmful-intent separation pre-generation, do not predict jailbreak success and can misallocate false positives toward attacks that would have failed. To address prompt-dependent measurement locations, it introduces Active Attention Probing to provide a fixed, content-independent coordinate and evaluates paired plain vs. wrapped prompts with real target-model completions. On Llama, wrapping increases harmful generations from 0.05 to 0.27 while harmful-intent AUROC drops from 0.936 to 0.803, and for wrapped harmful prompts the outcome AUROC is 0.220, with the reversal reproduced across models, attack families, judges, and alternative channels, and with distribution shift harming calibration/threshold transfer before ranking.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It challenges the common practice of using pre-generation intent scores as proxies for attack success and offers a measurement fix (AAP) with evidence of anti-correlation under wrapping, directly informing eval design and filter tuning for jailbreak defense.
evaluation.reason: Automated discovery and causal verification of spurious shortcuts in text classifiers is relevant to evaluation robustness and dataset contamination/shortcut mitigation.

evaluation.title: Tevatron-Elastic: A Unified Abstraction for Training Elastic Retrievers and Rerankers
evaluation.summary: Tevatron-Elastic introduces a unified abstraction that encapsulates three orthogonal elasticity axes for IR models—fewer layers, upper-layer token pruning, and shorter embeddings—so a single checkpoint supports multiple runtime sizes selected via a schedule. The abstraction applies uniformly to retrievers and rerankers, encoder and decoder backbones via HF interfaces, subsuming prior methods like Matryoshka embeddings, early exit, 2D Matryoshka (e.g., Starbucks), and layerwise token compression, and also enables Matryoshka LTC for jointly training multiple token-compression ratios in one retriever. Empirically, across 20 checkpoints, three backbones, and two tasks, they report smooth quality curves, near-single-size training cost, and controlled wallclock speedups, releasing the framework and checkpoints for elastic retrieval systems.
evaluation.why_it_matters: A clean, composable interface for multi-axis elasticity in retrievers/rerankers simplifies deployment-time cost/quality trade-offs and unifies techniques ML security and systems folks already use (early exit, Matryoshka, token compression) under one training/checkpoint regime.
evaluation.reason: Elastic retrievers/rerankers address scalable retrieval tradeoffs and dynamic model-size/runtime adaptation—useful for efficient RAG/agent pipelines and evaluation of retrieval components in security workflows.

evaluation.title: Capability-Routed Guard: Defending Large Reasoning Models Against Reasoning-Centric Jailbreaks
evaluation.summary: The paper introduces Capability-Routed Guard (CRG), a model-agnostic, inference-time guardrail for closed-source LRMs that reframes prompt defense as capability routing by constructing a trusted representation of authorized task, active context, safety evidence, and capability-transfer risk. CRG supports route-specific execution to block high-risk requests, constrain ambiguous ones, and forward low-risk requests via trusted active context, then applies TraceCheck for consistency with the authorized task and uses a restricted fallback to preserve utility for low-risk benign prompts. Experiments show CRG mitigates diverse reasoning-centric jailbreaks while preserving benign utility and avoiding over-refusals, with component analyses indicating complementary benefits and the importance of coordinated defenses for securing LRMs.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Directly targets reasoning-centric jailbreaks in LRMs with a practical, model-agnostic routing + verification pipeline that can be layered onto closed-source systems without weights or trace access.
evaluation.reason: Discussion of verification, contamination, and LLM-as-judge reliability informs benchmark trust and evaluation methods, important context for honest security/benchmarking practices.

evaluation.title: Beyond Solvability: Task Learnability as a Static Prior for LLM RL Post-Training
evaluation.summary: The paper introduces task learnability as a regime-conditional measure capturing how much tasks are expected to improve under a fixed LLM RL post-training setup, beyond snapshot solvability. They show learnability is reproducible across training contexts, predictive of downstream utility, and propose TrajVal, a probe-based estimator using a short probe run and two endpoint evaluations to approximate per-task learnability pre-training. TrajVal serves as a static prior for task sampling or as a multiplicative prior with online schedulers, improving data efficiency on math and logic benchmarks across model scales.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Offers a practical, pre-training prior for task selection in RL post-training that complements online schedulers, improving compute allocation for reasoning tasks.
evaluation.reason: Proposes task learnability as a static prior to improve RL post-training sampling—relevant to efficient RLHF/RL fine-tuning and evaluation of curricula for eliciting reasoning in LLMs (methodology applicable to red-teaming and costly post-training regimes).

evaluation.title: ProbGuard: Calibrated Safety Risk Estimation from LLM Output Distributions
evaluation.summary: ProbGuard reframes LLM safety assessment as probabilistic risk estimation over the model’s early output distribution rather than deterministic classification on completed token sequences. It estimates the probability of unsafe continuation via Monte Carlo over generated prefix distributions and calibrates this risk through post-training, enabling early stopping of unsafe generations. Empirically, it achieves the best calibration across nine model–dataset settings (average Brier and ECE reduced by 79.6% and 71.9% vs. the best baseline) and caps jailbreak attack success to ≤1% after only the first ten decoding steps.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It operationalizes distribution-aware, early-stage safety control with strong calibration—useful for red-teaming defenses, risk-sensitive deployment, and aligning with probabilistic guardrail research and time-series-style forecasting over generation trajectories.
evaluation.reason: Proposes a novel metric (feature nonlocality) to assess abstraction level of learned features from sparse autoencoders; useful for mechanistic interpretability and evaluating claims about high-level features relevant to jailbreak/mechanistic work.

evaluation.title: Weightless Fine-Tuning: Personalizing LLMs via Logit-Space Transport
evaluation.summary: The paper introduces Weightless Fine-Tuning (WFT), a training-free, decoding-time method that approximates SFT’s distributional effect by transporting supervised residuals from an author’s training sequence to a new prompt via a cross-prefix transport operator estimated from dropout-induced cross-covariance. WFT replaces gradient-based weight updates with logit-space corrections and, on three LaMP personalization benchmarks, achieves the best average performance, matches or exceeds SFT on individual tasks, and outperforms other lightweight baselines on average while using under 7% of the effective compute in a budget-controlled comparison. Logit-level analysis reports 0.875 cosine similarity between WFT- and SFT-induced logit shifts across 95% of next-token mass, indicating it captures SFT’s distributional effect without modifying weights.
evaluation.why_it_matters: A training-free, on-the-fly alternative to SFT that preserves personalization quality with minimal compute/storage has direct implications for secure, per-user adaptation and scalable deployment without per-user weight handling.
evaluation.reason: Decoding‑time personalization without weight updates could affect attack surfaces (e.g., personalization leakage) and enables efficient inference methods relevant to scalable red‑teaming.

evaluation.title: The Next Challenge for Agentic Cybersecurity: A Realistic, Contamination-Free Reverse Engineering Benchmark
evaluation.summary: The paper introduces SRE-Bench, a contamination-free reverse engineering benchmark built from scratch by experts, comprising 19 private real-world-scale programs (avg 16.9K LOC), 44 anti-analysis primitives, 262 binary instances, and 1572 deterministically graded tasks. Evaluating five frontier LLMs shows RE remains largely unsolved, with the strongest model scoring 61.4% per instance and fully solving only 31.5%, and agents exhibiting different sensitivities than humans to factors like compiler optimization and static linking. Ablations demonstrate that both contamination control and realistic scale are essential for valid evaluation, underscoring that strong source-code security capabilities do not transfer to binary analysis.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Offers a rigorous, contamination-controlled benchmark to stress-test agentic LLMs on binary RE at realistic scale—directly relevant to advancing secure agent capabilities beyond source-available settings.
evaluation.reason: Reverse‑engineering benchmark for agentic cybersecurity targets agent capabilities on binaries and contamination‑free evaluation, relevant to realistic red‑teaming and security evaluation.

evaluation.title: Task- and dataset-specific information in protein language models
evaluation.summary: Across 13 PLMs and 15 downstream tasks, intermediate-layer embeddings often outperform last-layer embeddings, contradicting the common practice of using the final layer. The layer at which task-relevant information concentrates depends on the task–pretraining alignment and the dataset: residue-level tasks see information accumulate with depth, while whole-protein performance is dataset-driven, with DMS favoring shallow layers and diverse natural proteins favoring deeper layers. PLM performance degrades markedly on tasks involving artificial proteins.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Highlights layer- and dataset-specific representation selection, informing secure model probing, adversarial evaluation, and transfer strategies analogous to layerwise selection in LLMs and time-series FMs.
evaluation.reason: Bilevel‑minimax formulation for transfer attacks improves black‑box adversarial transferability — relevant for adversarial robustness and attack methodology informing LLM security.

evaluation.title: DreamGuard: Efficient Runtime Guardrail for LLM Agents via Risk-Aware World Model
evaluation.summary: DreamGuard is a proactive runtime guardrail for LLM agents that uses a risk-aware world model to track a compact recurrent latent state over trajectories and forecast future latent states. From these forecasts, it derives immediate-hazard and prefix-risk evidence and fuses multi-horizon signals to decide on interventions before tool executions. Across four benchmarks and an online evaluation, DreamGuard outperforms generic, reactive, and proactive baselines with the best safety-utility trade-off and averages 25 ms end-to-end latency per call.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Introduces a trajectory-aware, low-latency guardrail with explicit risk modeling, aligning with interests in long-horizon safety for LLM agents and bridging to sequence modeling ideas from time series foundation models.
evaluation.reason: Adaptive allocation across model populations for LLM-driven evolutionary search is relevant for cost-efficient red-teaming/evolutionary program search, but more about budgeting than core security.

evaluation.title: SkillTFM: Gated Skill Evolution for Training-Free Adaptation of Tabular Foundation Models
evaluation.summary: The paper introduces SkillTFM, a training-free adaptation system for tabular foundation models that replaces parameter updates with gated evolution of agentic skills. It uses a verifiable, extensible skill bank combining boundary evidence identification to characterize task structure and base-model failures with gated skill evolution to retrieve and extend reusable skills under explicit validation. In simulated boundary settings and real-world electricity-price forecasting, SkillTFM improves AUC by 0.128–0.142, elevating nonlinear-boundary AUC from 0.699 to 0.898, and shows effectiveness across different TFM backbones.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It proposes a security-adjacent, verifiable skill-gating mechanism for training-free adaptation under distribution shift, echoing modular skill libraries and guarded tool-use in LLMs while targeting tabular/time-series TFMs.
evaluation.reason: Empirical study of self-pretraining for medical time series—useful data on pretraining benefits and transfer in noisy, multimodal TS settings though domain-specific.

evaluation.title: LabelFusion-TS: Fusing Large Language Models, Transformer Encoders, and Financial Time Series for Monetary-Policy Stance Classification
evaluation.summary: The paper introduces LabelFusion-TS, which combines a fine-tuned RoBERTa encoder, a prompted LLM, and an ensemble of time-series transformers over pre-publication market series via a small voting network to classify FOMC sentences as hawkish, dovish, or neutral. Due to limited human labels (~1k sentences), the RoBERTa encoder is first pre-trained on LLM-generated weak labels and then fine-tuned on human annotations. Trained on data up to 2015 and evaluated on 2015–2022, the fused system attains 70.2% weighted F1, surpassing a zero-shot LLM at 64.1% and overtaking it with as few as 240 human-labeled sentences.
evaluation.why_it_matters: It demonstrates measurable gains from fusing market time series with LLM/text encoders for monetary-policy stance classification, highlighting a practical multimodal path beyond text-only classifiers.
evaluation.reason: Multimodal fusion of financial time series with LLMs for stance classification touches the reader's TSFM interest (benchmarks/architectures) and evaluation, though it's a narrow financial NLP application.

evaluation.title: Analysis of Federated Aggregation under Model Poisoning and Backdoor Attacks: A Reconstructed Cross-Dataset and Cross-Architecture Benchmark
evaluation.summary: This work reconstructs a 500-cell federated aggregation benchmark across five methods, five datasets, five architectures, and four conditions (clean, sign-flipping, Gaussian, BadNets), recovering 454 original runs and 36 repairs/reruns, with 10 SVHN cells covered only by summary provenance. Trimmed Mean has the best clean macro-mean accuracy and lowest mean within-task rank, while Krum shows the top recorded accuracy under sign-flipping and Gaussian, and these rankings persist when restricted to fully logged task pairs. Audits reveal the BadNets metric is actually TTLR (all test inputs triggered) and a FedPARETO pathway where reported predictive summaries may not match the corrupted updates used for aggregation, so results are descriptive within recorded configs rather than universal robustness claims.
evaluation.why_it_matters: Highlights reproducibility gaps, metric mis-specification (TTLR), and aggregation/provenance pitfalls that can confound robustness claims in federated settings relevant to secure FL and poisoning/backdoor evaluation.
evaluation.reason: Cross‑dataset benchmark for federated aggregation under poisoning/backdoors informs robust evaluation and threat models though it's more federated learning than LLM‑specific.

longform.title: Intern-S2-Preview: Scientific Agentic Foundation Model
longform.summary: Intern-S2-Preview introduces scientific agentic foundation models trained via multimodal pretraining on rendered scientific documents, interleaved image-text, and diverse scientific corpora, followed by a unified post-training stack of SFT, scalable multi-task RL, black- and white-box agentic RL, and on-policy distillation. The pipeline adds practical rollout/training techniques—partial rollout with off-policy correction, adaptive length regularization, online speculative decoding, robust multi-task optimization, and trace-aware experience assembly—and explores architecture-level extensions: a 397B model with time series modules for efficient long-sequence understanding and numerical forecasting, plus a separate Memory Decoder path for rapid specialization without changing the frozen backbone. Evaluations report competitive or leading results across scientific, multimodal, agentic, and general-purpose benchmarks, with time-series gains on SciTS and a MemDec-4B extension improving Biology-Instructions average from 56.92 to 60.32 without modifying the 397B backbone.
longform.why_it_matters: Brings a concrete agentic RL + multimodal + TS forecasting stack with stability tricks and a memory-augmented specialization path relevant to secure tool-use agents and time-series LLMs.
longform.reason: Agentic multimodal scientific foundation model work intersects with agentic-system attack surfaces and long-horizon reasoning, relevant for security analysis though not focused on adversarial robustness.
